summary:
Papua stands under the national framework of Indonesia, a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, this effectively criminalises all consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates that prosecutions are selective rather than systematic. Two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, carry their own provisions against same-sex sexual activity, and in Aceh two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025 under provincial religious law that reaches anyone present, including foreign visitors. Papua has no equivalent provincial criminal provision in the sourced record, but customary laws may apply alongside the national code.

Identity documents are a documented access point. Since June 2021 the Indonesian Ministry of Home Affairs has run an outreach programme issuing identity papers (KTP) to transgender Indonesians, and Papua is among the provinces where trans residents have received them, alongside Banten, West Java, Central Java, East Java, North Sumatra, South Sumatra, South Sulawesi and Lampung. Only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors are recognised, and the birth sex is printed unless a court order was obtained beforehand. A trans person in Papua may therefore hold correctly issued identity documents while remaining subject to the national framework that criminalises their relationships.

Official policy at national level frames LGBTQ+ people as a security matter. A presidential decree issued by President Prabowo Subianto in October 2025 lists nonmilitary threats and places LGBTQ+ people within national defence policy as risks to be monitored and controlled. Reporting from August 2026 ties that framing to a wave of vigilante attacks on transgender women, with mobs attacking trans people as anti-LGBTQ+ attitudes are codified into law; commentators quoted by ABC News state that the regulation moved hostile rhetoric into the official doctrine of national defence policy.

The detention environment in Papua is documented and severe, though the evidence describes general-population risk rather than trans-specific targeting. A TAPOL briefing of July 2025 records 138 acts of torture or ill-treatment in detention by police and military in Maybrat and the Central Highlands between September 2021 and the first quarter of 2025, with almost no consequences; deaths during torture are documented in the operation areas, and the incidents are catalogued on the 'Papuans Behind Bars' database. Victims were mostly males under 24, plus 7 women and 7 minors, and arrests were largely for alleged armed-group links or participation in demonstrations.

The Human Rights Monitor Papua Quarterly Report of 31 October 2025 records killings, arbitrary detentions, torture and arrests of protesters alongside the failure of accountability mechanisms as security forces expand across the territory, with a healthcare crisis under scrutiny. For a trans visitor, contact with security forces in the highland districts therefore carries a documented risk of arbitrary detention and mistreatment with little prospect of redress, and the surveillance and deployment environment raises the chance of being noticed and questioned.
tangentialFactors:
Security force operations in Papua have produced fatalities and mass detentions without trans-specific findings. The Q3 2025 reporting period covered fatal shootings, arbitrary detentions and the arrest of protesters, and a further surge in military deployments, fatal shootings and arbitrary detentions has been recorded from August 2025 together with internal displacement.

At national level, venue raids demonstrate the enforcement method used against LGBTQ+ people. On 22 June 2025 Indonesian police raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after public reports of a "gay party" and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman. Amnesty International's Deputy Director Wirya Adiwena described the operation as a blatant violation of human rights and privacy and stated that the gathering violated no law.

There is a directly documented death of a trans traveller in Indonesian custody. Rodrigo Ventocilla Ventosilla, a Harvard student and trans activist from Peru, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges while on honeymoon in Bali in 2022. During a WhatsApp call, his mother in Lima was told that authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody; his mother alleges that police beat him, while Indonesian police have denied that violence was used.
localsOnly:
Trans residents of Papua have received identity papers through the national outreach programme administered by the Ministry of Home Affairs since June 2021. Only two sex descriptors are available on the card, and the sex recorded at birth appears unless a court order was obtained in advance, so corrected documents depend on judicial action rather than administrative process.

Residents live under the national penal code provisions on sex outside marriage, under which consensual same-sex relations are effectively criminalised, and may also be subject to customary law. Arrests in the province have been made largely for alleged armed-group links or for taking part in demonstrations, and accountability mechanisms for mistreatment in detention have failed, with recorded incidents carried out by police and military and almost no consequences. Trans residents are therefore exposed to the same documented detention risk as the wider population, against a background in which national policy classifies LGBTQ+ people as a security concern.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources disagree on the penalty for sex outside marriage: the national framework describes up to two years' imprisonment, while the inventory of the 2022 penal-code amendment states up to one year. The figure should be treated as unresolved pending the text of the code as promulgated.

No Papua-specific incident of violence against a trans person, no trans-specific arrest and no local enforcement action against a venue or individual is sourced for this province. The recorded torture and detention data describe a general-population pattern and are not attributed to trans victims. Whether trans visitors' foreign documents carrying an amended or non-binary sex marker are accepted at identity checks in Papua is not sourced, and the interaction between customary law and trans people in the province is likewise not documented in the available material. The Q3 2025 provincial reporting carries no trans or LGBTI findings.
